l: Opheltes, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Opheltes is the infant son of Eurydice and Lycurgus, and Hypsipyle nurses him. After Hypsipyle leaves him to show the champions the spring, a serpent kills him; the champions bury him and call him Archemorus.

l: serpent, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: A serpent kills Opheltes while Hypsipyle is showing the champions the spring. Adrastus and his companions kill the serpent.

l: Archemorus, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Archemorus is the name given to Opheltes after his death. Amphiaraus says that the child's death is a sign foretelling the future.

l: Nemean Games, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: The champions establish the Nemean Games in honor of Opheltes, whom they call Archemorus. Adrastus wins the horse race, Eteoclus the foot race, Tydeus boxing, Amphiaraus leaping and quoit-throwing, Laodocus the javelin, Polynices wrestling, and Parthenopaeus archery.

l: necklace, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Polynices carries the necklace and robe to Argos and gives the necklace to Eriphyle. Eriphyle accepts it and persuades Amphiaraus to join the war.

l: war against Thebes, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Adrastus gathers the Seven Champions for the war against Thebes. Amphiaraus initially opposes the expedition because he foresees the deaths of its participants except Adrastus, but Eriphyle persuades him to join; the army later proceeds toward Thebes.

l: The Library, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: The Argives armed themselves and approached the walls of Thebes, with seven leaders stationed at the seven gates. Eteocles armed the Thebans, appointed matching leaders, arranged the battle, and sought through divination to learn how the Thebans could defeat the enemy. The Theban seer Tiresias was blind but possessed prophetic abilities, and different accounts explained his blindness and powers. One account says Athena blinded him after he saw her naked, while another says Hera blinded him after he judged that women experience greater pleasure in intercourse, and Zeus gave him prophetic power.

l: Argives, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: The Argives armed themselves and approached the walls of Thebes. Their seven leaders were stationed at the seven gates: Adrastus, Capaneus, Amphiaraus, Hippomedon, Polynices, Parthenopaeus, and Tydeus.

l: Thebans, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: The Thebans were armed by Eteocles, who appointed leaders corresponding in number to the enemy leaders and arranged them for battle.

l: Eteocles, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Eteocles armed the Thebans, appointed matching leaders, arranged the battle, and sought through divination to learn how the Thebans could defeat the Argives.

l: Tiresias, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Tiresias was a Theban seer, son of Everes and the nymph Chariclo, descended from Udaeus the Spartoi. He was blind but understood the voices of birds, possessed prophetic power, and was granted long life.

l: Chariclo, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Chariclo was a nymph, the mother of Tiresias, and was dear to Athena. In the account attributed to Pherecydes, she asked Athena to restore Tiresias's sight after he had been blinded.

l: Athena, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: According to Pherecydes, Athena blinded Tiresias after he saw her naked. She could not restore his sight, but cleansed his ears so that he could understand every bird's voice and gave him a cornel-wood staff.

l: Hera, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Hera questioned Tiresias with Zeus about whether men or women take greater pleasure in intercourse. After Tiresias said that women experience nine parts of pleasure out of ten, Hera blinded him.

l: Zeus, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Zeus questioned Tiresias with Hera about sexual pleasure. After Hera blinded Tiresias because of his answer, Zeus gave him prophetic power and made him long-lived.

l: Thebes, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Thebes was approached by the armed Argives, who took positions at its seven gates. Its defenders were armed and organized by Eteocles.

l: Argive attack on Thebes, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: The Argive attack began with the Argives arming themselves and approaching the walls of Thebes. Seven named Argive leaders were assigned to the seven gates.

l: battle between the Argives and Thebans, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: The battle was being prepared: the Argives took positions at the gates, while Eteocles armed and organized the Thebans. The text does not yet describe the battle's outcome.

l: divination, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Eteocles resorted to divination to learn how the Thebans might overcome the Argives. Tiresias, who was a seer, is then described in connection with prophetic knowledge.

l: blindness of Tiresias, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Different accounts explain the blindness of Tiresias. One says that Athena blinded him after he saw her naked; another says that Hera blinded him after he answered her dispute with Zeus about sexual pleasure.

l: prophetic power of Tiresias, The Library, 6 ᾿Αργεῖοε δὲ καθοπλισθέντες προσήεσαν τοῖς
s: Tiresias possessed prophetic power despite his blindness. Athena is said to have enabled him to understand every bird's voice, and Zeus is said to have granted him the power of divination.

l: The Library, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Tiresias tells the Thebans that they will win if Menoeceus, son of Creon, sacrifices himself to Ares, and Menoeceus kills himself before the gates. During the battle at Thebes, the Cadmeans are driven back, Zeus strikes Capaneus with a thunderbolt, and the Argives begin to flee. Eteocles and Polynices fight a single combat over the kingdom of Thebes and kill each other. Melanippus wounds Tydeus, Athena attempts to make Tydeus immortal, but withholds the gift after Tydeus consumes Melanippus's brains; Zeus later makes Amphiaraus immortal after the earth swallows him with his chariot and charioteer.

l: Tiresias, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Tiresias tells the Thebans that they will be victorious if Menoeceus offers himself as a sacrifice to Ares. Zeus also gives Tiresias the art of soothsaying, while Hera blinds him.

l: Zeus, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Zeus gives Tiresias the art of soothsaying. During the battle, Zeus strikes Capaneus with a thunderbolt and later cleaves the earth so that Amphiaraus disappears, after which he makes Amphiaraus immortal.

l: Thebans, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: The Thebans seek counsel from Tiresias before the battle. They are told that victory depends on Menoeceus sacrificing himself to Ares.

l: Thebes, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Thebes is the place whose defenders fight the Argives. Its walls are reached during the battle, and the struggle for its kingdom leads to the deaths of Eteocles and Polynices.

l: Menoeceus, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Menoeceus, son of Creon, kills himself before the gates after hearing Tiresias's prophecy. His self-sacrifice is presented as the condition for the Thebans' victory.

l: self-sacrifice of Menoeceus, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: The self-sacrifice of Menoeceus consists of his offering himself to Ares by killing himself before the gates. Tiresias says that it will bring victory to the Thebans.

l: battle between the Argives and Thebans, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: In the battle at Thebes, the Cadmeans are chased as far as the walls, Capaneus climbs toward the walls, and Zeus strikes him with a thunderbolt. The Argives then turn to flee, while Eteocles and Polynices fight over the kingdom.

l: Cadmeans, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: The Cadmeans are driven in pursuit as far as the walls during the battle. Their opponents subsequently turn to flee after Zeus strikes Capaneus.

l: Capaneus, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Capaneus seizes a ladder and climbs toward the walls. Zeus strikes him with a thunderbolt, after which the Argives turn to flee.

l: Argives, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: The Argives fight against the Cadmeans at Thebes. After Capaneus is struck by Zeus and many of them have fallen, they turn to flee.

l: Eteocles, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Eteocles fights Polynices in a single combat over the kingdom of Thebes. The two brothers kill each other.

l: Polynices, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Polynices fights Eteocles in a single combat over the kingdom of Thebes. The two brothers kill each other.

l: kingdom of Thebes, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: The kingdom of Thebes is contested by Eteocles and Polynices in a single combat. The contest ends with both of them dead.

l: single combat of Eteocles and Polynices, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: The single combat of Eteocles and Polynices is fought by agreement of both armies over the kingdom. Each brother kills the other.

l: Melanippus, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Melanippus, one of the sons of Astacus, wounds Tydeus in the belly. Amphiaraus cuts off Melanippus's head and gives it to Tydeus.

l: Tydeus, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Tydeus is wounded in the belly by Melanippus and lies half dead. He splits open Melanippus's head and consumes the brains, causing Athena to withhold the medicine intended to make him immortal.

l: Athena, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Athena brings a medicine obtained from Zeus that she intends to use to make Tydeus immortal. After seeing Tydeus consume Melanippus's brains, she is disgusted and withholds the benefit.

l: Amphiaraus, The Library, Οὗτος οὖν Θηβαίοις μαντενομένοις 3 εἶπε νική-
s: Amphiaraus hates Tydeus for persuading the Argives to march to Thebes against his advice. He cuts off Melanippus's head and gives it to Tydeus, then flees beside the river Ismenus before Zeus opens the earth and swallows him with his chariot and charioteer; Zeus makes him immortal.

l: The Library, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Creon of Thebes refused burial to the Argive dead, but Antigone buried Polynices and was buried alive, after which Adrastus appealed to Athens and Theseus led the Athenians to recover the dead. Ten years later, the Epigoni attacked Thebes under Alcmaeon, defeated its defenders, and caused the Thebans to flee; the Argives then destroyed the city and dedicated spoils, including Manto, to Apollo. Alcmaeon later killed Eriphyle, was pursued for the killing, and after successive purifications received Callirrhoe from Achelous. His sons eventually avenged his death, dedicated the robe and necklace of Eriphyle at Delphi, and colonized Acarnania.

l: Creon, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: After succeeding to the kingdom of Thebes, Creon cast out the Argive dead unburied and ordered that no one bury them. He set watchmen, and after Antigone buried Polynices, he had her interred alive.

l: Thebes, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Thebes was attacked by the Athenians under Theseus and later by the Epigoni. After the death of Laodamas, its inhabitants fled, and the Argives entered the city, collected its booty, and destroyed its walls.

l: Argive dead, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: The Argive dead were denied burial by Creon. At the appeal of Adrastus, the Athenians under Theseus recovered them and gave them to their relatives for burial.

l: Antigone, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Antigone, one of the daughters of Oedipus, secretly stole and buried the body of Polynices. Creon detected her and buried her alive in the grave.

l: Polynices, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Polynices's body was left unburied by Creon. Antigone secretly took the body and buried it.

l: Adrastus, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Adrastus alone escaped from the first expedition against Thebes, saved by his horse Arion. He fled to Athens, sought refuge at the altar of Mercy, and asked that the Argive dead be buried.

l: Athens, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Athens received Adrastus as a suppliant at the altar of Mercy. Its citizens marched with Theseus, captured Thebes, and secured the Argive dead for burial.

l: Theseus, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Theseus led the Athenians in their expedition against Thebes. They captured the city and gave the Argive dead to their relatives for burial.

l: Epigoni, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: The Epigoni were the sons of those who had died in the first expedition against Thebes. Ten years later they marched against Thebes to avenge their fathers, choosing Alcmaeon as their leader.

l: war against Thebes, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: The Epigoni first ravaged the villages around Thebes and then fought the Thebans under Laodamas. After Laodamas was killed, the Thebans fled, the Argives entered Thebes, took its booty, and destroyed its walls.

l: Alcmaeon, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Alcmaeon led the Epigoni after Apollo predicted victory under his leadership, although he initially wished to punish Eriphyle before leading the army. He killed Laodamas, later killed Eriphyle on Apollo's instruction, and was pursued by the Fury of his mother's murder. After purification by Phegeus and Achelous, he married Arsinoe and later Callirrhoe; he was eventually killed by the sons of Phegeus.

l: Eriphyle, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Eriphyle received the robe of Eriphyle from Thersander and persuaded her sons to join the expedition against Thebes. After Alcmaeon learned that she had been bribed, Apollo instructed him to kill her, and he did so, either alone or with Amphilochus.

l: robe of Eriphyle, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: The robe of Eriphyle was given by Thersander to Eriphyle and influenced her to persuade her sons to join the war. Alcmaeon later gave it to Arsinoe, falsely claimed that he needed it for dedication at Delphi, and ultimately had it dedicated there by his sons according to Achelous's instruction.

l: necklace, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: The necklace of Eriphyle was given by Alcmaeon to Arsinoe after his purification by Phegeus. Alcmaeon later obtained it again by claiming that it had to be dedicated at Delphi, and his sons eventually dedicated it there according to Achelous's instruction.

l: Tiresias, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Tiresias advised the Thebans to send a herald to the Argives and flee themselves. He died after drinking from the spring called Tilphussa while the Thebans were fleeing.

l: Apollo, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Apollo predicted victory for the Epigoni under Alcmaeon's leadership and later instructed Alcmaeon to kill Eriphyle. The Argives dedicated part of the booty from Thebes and Manto to Apollo at Delphi.

l: Phegeus, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Phegeus purified Alcmaeon at Psophis and gave him his daughter Arsinoe in marriage. He believed Alcmaeon's claim that the necklace and robe were needed for dedication at Delphi, but ordered his sons to kill Alcmaeon after learning that he intended to give them to Callirrhoe.

l: Psophis, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Psophis received Alcmaeon when he came to Phegeus for purification. Later, after the sons of Alcmaeon killed Phegeus and his wife, the Psophidians pursued them but were defeated and fled.

l: Achelous, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Achelous was the destination to which Alcmaeon was sent by an oracle because the land had become barren on his account. He purified Alcmaeon, gave him Callirrhoe as a wife, and instructed Alcmaeon's sons to dedicate the necklace and robe at Delphi.

l: Callirrhoe, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Callirrhoe, the daughter of Achelous, became Alcmaeon's wife after his purification by Achelous. She demanded the necklace and robe and, after Alcmaeon's death, asked that her sons by Alcmaeon become full-grown so that they could avenge him.

l: Acarnania, The Library, VII. Κρέων δὲ τὴν Θηβαίων βασιλείαν παραλα-
s: Acarnania was colonized by the sons of Alcmaeon after they avenged their father's death and dedicated the necklace and robe at Delphi according to Achelous's instruction.

l: The Library, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: The unit recounts the lineage of Pelasgus through his son Lycaon and Lycaon’s fifty sons, including Nyctimus and Maenalus. Zeus tests the sons’ impiety by appearing as a day-labourer, but they serve him a sacrifice mixed with the entrails of a murdered child. Zeus overturns the table, destroys Lycaon and his sons except Nyctimus, and the flood of Deucalion occurs during Nyctimus’s reign. The unit also relates the story of Callisto, whom Zeus seduces and transforms into a bear before placing her among the stars.

l: Pelasgus, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Pelasgus is identified as the father of Lycaon. Acusilaus says that he was a son of Zeus and Niobe, while Hesiod says that he was born from the soil.

l: Zeus, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Zeus tests the impiety of Lycaon’s sons by appearing in the likeness of a day-labourer. After they serve him a child’s entrails mixed with sacrificial offerings, he overturns the table and strikes Lycaon and his sons with thunderbolts, except Nyctimus; he later has intercourse with Callisto while disguised as Artemis or Apollo, and transforms her into a bear to conceal her from Hera.

l: Lycaon, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Lycaon is the son of Pelasgus and rules the Arcadians. He fathers fifty sons by many women, and Zeus destroys him with a thunderbolt after the impious banquet prepared by his sons.

l: Nyctimus, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Nyctimus is the youngest of Lycaon’s sons and is spared when Zeus destroys Lycaon and the other sons. He succeeds to the kingdom, and the flood of Deucalion occurs during his reign.

l: Maenalus, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Maenalus is one of Lycaon’s sons and is identified as the elder brother who advises the preparation of the impious sacrifice for Zeus.

l: Deucalion’s flood, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Deucalion’s flood occurs after Nyctimus takes over the kingdom. Some accounts attribute it to the impiety of Lycaon’s sons.

l: Callisto, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Callisto is said by Eumelus and others to be Lycaon’s daughter, though other accounts describe her as a nymph or as the daughter of Nycteus or Ceteus. She is a companion of Artemis who swears to remain a virgin, but Zeus sleeps with her against her will; she is transformed into a bear, and Zeus later places her among the stars.

l: Artemis, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Artemis has Callisto as a hunting companion, and Callisto wears the same clothing as Artemis and swears to remain a virgin. Hera persuades Artemis to shoot Callisto as a wild animal, although another account says that Artemis shoots her because Callisto did not preserve her virginity.

l: Hera, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Hera is the one from whom Zeus wishes to conceal his union with Callisto. She persuades Artemis to shoot Callisto as a wild animal.

l: impiety, The Library, VIII. ᾿Επανάγωμεν δὲ νῦν πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν Πε-
s: Lycaon’s sons are described as surpassing all people in pride and impiety. Zeus tests their impiety, and their treatment of him at the banquet leads to the destruction of Lycaon and his sons; some accounts also connect their impiety with Deucalion’s flood.

l: The Library, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Arcas had two sons, Elatus and Aphidas, who divided the land, though Elatus held all the power. Elatus and Aphidas had descendants including Aleus, whose daughter Auge was seduced by Heracles and later married Teuthras, ruler of Mysia. Auge's exposed infant was named Telephus, was raised by herdsmen, and eventually became Teuthras's adopted son and successor. The unit also recounts the upbringing, contests, race, marriage, and later fate of Atalanta, including her pursuit by Melanion with golden apples from Aphrodite.

l: Arcas, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Arcas had two sons, Elatus and Aphidas. They divided the land between them, although Elatus held all the power.

l: Elatus, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Elatus was a son of Arcas and a brother of Aphidas. He received a share of the land but held all the power, and he fathered Stymphalus and Pereus.

l: Aphidas, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Aphidas was a son of Arcas and a brother of Elatus. He fathered Aleus and Stheneboea.

l: Aleus, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Aleus was a son of Aphidas. By Neaera, he had a daughter, Auge, and two sons, Cepheus and Lycurgus.

l: Auge, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Auge was Aleus's daughter and held the priesthood of Athena. After being seduced by Heracles, she hid her baby in Athena's precinct; when the land became barren and the impiety in the precinct was revealed, her father handed her over to Nauplius for execution. Teuthras received and married her.

l: Hercules, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Heracles seduced Auge, who consequently bore a baby and hid it in Athena's precinct.

l: Athena, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Athena had a precinct in which Auge held the priesthood. The exposure of Auge's baby there was regarded as an impiety when the land became barren.

l: Teuthras, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Teuthras was the ruler of Mysia. He received and married Auge, and later adopted her son Telephus, who succeeded him as ruler when he died.

l: Mysia, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Mysia was ruled by Teuthras. Telephus went there after receiving information from the god at Delphi and became Teuthras's adopted son and successor.

l: Telephus, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Telephus was Auge's exposed baby, who was suckled by a doe on Mount Parthenius and raised by the herdsmen of Corythus. He sought his parents, went to Delphi, and then traveled to Mysia, where he became Teuthras's adopted son and succeeded him as ruler.

l: Iasus, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Iasus was the father of Atalanta according to the account presented here. Hesiod and others instead said that Atalanta's father was Schoeneus.

l: Melanion, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Melanion pursued Atalanta in her race for marriage, using golden apples from Aphrodite to distract her and win. He married Atalanta, and she bore him Parthenopaeus; another account names Ares as the father instead.

l: Atalanta, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Atalanta was exposed by her father because he wanted male children, was suckled by a she-bear, and was raised by hunters. She remained a virgin and a skilled armed huntress, killed the centaurs Rhoecus and Hylaeus when they tried to force her, joined the hunt for the Calydonian boar, and defeated Peleus in wrestling. She later lost her marriage race to Melanion after stopping to pick up the golden apples, married him, and was transformed with him into lions after they had intercourse in the precinct of Zeus.

l: Aphrodite, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Aphrodite supplied Melanion with golden apples, which he threw down while Atalanta pursued him.

l: Atalanta's race, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Atalanta's wooers raced from a starting point while she pursued them in armor. A wooer who was caught was to die, while one who escaped was to marry her; after many had died, Melanion won by using golden apples.

l: golden apples, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: The golden apples came from Aphrodite. Melanion threw them down during the race, and Atalanta stopped to pick them up, allowing him to defeat her.

l: Athena’s precinct, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Auge hid her baby in Athena's precinct, where she held the priesthood. When the land became barren, oracles declared that an impiety existed there, leading to the discovery of the baby and Auge's punishment.

l: wooers, The Library, IX. ᾿Αρκάδος δὲ καὶ Λεανείρας τῆς ᾿Αμύκλου
s: Atalanta's wooers had to race against her to obtain marriage. Those whom she caught were to be killed, and many had already died before Melanion entered the race and won.

This is a travel and antiquarian account of Greece, organized as a journey through Attica, Corinthia, Laconia, Messenia, and Elis. It describes harbours, roads, towns, sanctuaries, temples, statues, paintings, tombs, rivers, customs, festivals, games, local myths, and political memories, continually joining visible monuments to stories of gods, heroes, artists, rulers, and wars. It begins in Attica, above all Athens: its approaches, Acropolis, Parthenon, courts, theatre, Painted Chamber, temples, graves, and surrounding places such as Marathon, Eleusis, Megara, Salamis, and Oropus. Athene, Theseus, Demeter, Triptolemus, Apollo, and Zeus dominate its sacred traditions; Themistocles, Pericles, Plato, Demosthenes, Adrian, and artists including Phidias, Praxiteles, and Euphranor figure in its civic memory. Interwoven historical digressions trace Alexander’s successors, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Lysimachus, and Pyrrhus, ending in Pyrrhus’s death at Argos. The route then enters Corinth and Sicyon, recounting Corinth’s destruction and rebuilding, its Isthmian sites, rulers, and myths, before moving through Phlius, Nemea, Mycenæ, Tiryns, Argos, Epidaurus, Ægina, Trœzen, and Hermione. Major themes are the Argive royal traditions, the return of the Heraclidæ, Theseus, and the healing sanctuary of Æsculapius at Epidaurus. In Laconia, the account combines Sparta’s legendary origins, kings, Lycurgan institutions, wars, and decline with a detailed survey of Spartan monuments and rituals, including the contests of youths and the cult of Orthian Artemis. It extends through Amyclæ, Therapne, Gythium, Cythera, Tænarum, and other coastal places. Messenia centers on resistance to Lacedæmon. The wars of Euphaes, Aristodemus, and especially Aristomenes lead from Amphea and Ithome to the fall of Eira, exile, settlement at Zancle, and eventual restoration of Messene by Epaminondas and the Thebans. The final books reach Elis and Olympia. They recount Elis’s history and the revival, contests, officials, rites, cheating penalties, monuments, temples, and treasures of the Olympian games. Olympian Zeus, Pelops, Hercules, athletes such as Polydamas, Euthymus, Diagoras, and Theagenes, and the many statues and offerings at Altis dominate the close, which ends with Elis, Cyllene, and the boundary with Achaia.

Pausanias is presented both as an author-narrator and as a historical figure: regent for Plistarchus, leader of the Lacedæmonians at Platæa, sparer of a Coan woman, and later troubled by killing Cleonice at Byzantium. He is buried among the tombs of Pausanias and Leonidas. In his account, he describes Attica’s places and traditions with attention to inquiry, and Olympia’s statues and votive offerings rather than all victors. The records also distinguish a later Pausanias, son of Plistoanax, who opposed the Thirty Tyrants and retired to Tegea.

Attica is Attic soil, a promontory region on the mainland of Greece facing the Cyclades and the Ægean sea. Formerly called Actæa, it was said to be named for Atthis, daughter of Cranaus. It contains Athens, Sunium, the harbours of Piraeus, Munychia, and Phalerum, fortified places including Panactus, Salamis, Eleusis, and Munychia, and the setting of the Marathonian bull. Its numerous townships, mountains, islands, temples, altars, tombs, and monuments include Pentelicus, Parnes, Hymettus, and Alimus.

woos Helen [according to the narrator] Patroclus is identified as the person who killed Las, contrary to the local tradition that attributed the killing to Achilles. The text says that Patroclus, rather than Achilles, wooed Helen.

Ptolemy, said to be son of Philip by the Macedonians and putatively of Lagus, became king and ruler of Egypt after Alexander’s death. He supported dividing Alexander’s dominions, seized Egypt, killed Cleomenes, Argæus, Eurydice’s son, and another brother, and brought Alexander the Great’s corpse from Memphis. He expanded into Syria, Phœnicia, and Cyprus, resisted invasions, allied against Antigonus, aided Rhodes and Pyrrhus, opposed Magas and Antiochus I, and used then abandoned Galatian mercenaries. He married his sister Arsinoe but had sons by Lysimachus’s daughter.

Antigonus is a king of the Macedonians, recorded as both son and father of Demetrius. He opposed Ptolemy, seized Syria and Phœnicia, and put them under Demetrius, but failed in campaigns against Egypt and Rhodes. He attacked and invested Athens, made peace, placed then withdrew a garrison. Later he fought Lysimachus, Cassander, and Seleucus, lost most forces and power, and died. After failing to reinforce Pyrrhus, his troops were defeated and Upper Macedonia and Thessaly were taken.

The Athenians are a political and religious community centered on Athens, with older resources and institutions including silver mines at Laurium, Phalerum as their ancient port, Piraeus as their principal port under Themistocles, a temple common to all gods, and government by the code of Draco. They are distinguished above all by exceptional religious zeal: they are said to surpass other Greeks in it, first called Athene the worker, first worshipped the mutilated Hermæ, kept the God of the Zealous with them, treated the Ilissus as sacred, and preserved shrines, monuments, heroes, and divine honours for Ajax and Eurysaces. Their history unfolds through warfare, alliances, civic expansion, reversals, and recovery. They fought Persians, Macedonians, Galati, and others; defended Thermopylæ against the Galati; abandoned Athens before a Persian land attack while sending women and children to Troezen; and commemorated Marathon with tombs, honours, and a trophy. They fought Eleusinians, then incorporated Eleusis politically while leaving its Mysteries privately managed; expelled Æginetans from Ægina; claimed Megara and lost it to the Peloponnesians; and at times were surpassed by Æginetans at sea. They resisted Cleomenes and Isagoras’ dominion, fought with the Thebans at Haliartus, were listed second among the states at Platæa, and made a thirty-year peace with the Lacedæmonians after reducing Eubœa. Their relations with the Lacedæmonians alternated between aid and distrust: they assisted at Ithome but were dismissed as suspected revolutionaries, became friendly with the Argives, aided Messenians, gave them Naupactus, and commemorated Sphacteria with a brazen Victory. After Alexander’s death they initiated rebellion against Macedonian rule, urged other cities to join, and chose Leosthenes. They later endured garrisons and imposed rulers, but under Olympiodorus defeated the Macedonians and recovered Athens, Piraeus, and Munychia. They also received aid from Ptolemy I Soter and an Egyptian fleet, honoured benefactors and leaders with statues, and remained divided when Aristion preferred Mithridates while more respectable Athenians joined the Romans.

Piraeus, once a township, became a port under Themistocles, arranged with three harbours, ship stations, his tomb, temples, paintings, and porticoes; Conon erected a temple of Aphrodite. Later Macedonian forces held it, Demetrius did not promptly return it after Lachares fled, and Olympiodorus recovered it with Munychia.

is_a port [before Themistocles made Piraeus the port] Phalerum was the Athenians’ port before Themistocles established Piraeus, because it was nearer to Athens. Menestheus was said to have sailed from there to Troy, and the area contained temples of Artemis, Demeter, Sciradian Athene, and Zeus, as well as several altars.

Themistocles made Piraeus Athens’ port for its convenience and three harbours, fought Xerxes and the Medes in a great sea-fight, and built walls after the Persian defeat. The walls were later pulled down; his tomb stood at the largest harbour, and his sons returned from exile to dedicate his painting.

Theseus is a hero of Athenian tradition, also associated with other places and competing accounts. He was identified as the son of Aegeus through shoes and a sword found beneath Theseus’ rock. His career includes being acquitted at the Delphinium for justifiable homicide, purification at Milichian Zeus after killing the progeny of Phytalus, and the killing or defeat of dangerous figures including Sinis, Polypemon, Cercyon, Sciron, and Timalcus. The account credits him with defeating Cercyon by skill, making wrestling a science, and establishing training schools. His most notable exploit is presented as his return from Crete after killing Asterion amid the hidden dangers of the labyrinth; he is also said to have fought the Minotaur. After returning, he built Artemis the Saviour. He sailed from Phalerum to avenge Androgeos, fought Amazons, and may have carried off Antiope or received her help in taking Themiscyra. He recovered Minos’s ring from the sea and received a golden crown from Amphitrite. In Athens he was portrayed as restoring political equality and was believed by popular tradition to support Demos. When he combined the Athenians into one city, he established worship of Persuasion. Although one tradition called him king, this is rejected as untrue. Later he was imprisoned by the king of Thesprotia at Cichyrus, was killed on Scyrus, and his bones were subsequently conveyed to Athens, where he had a shrine. Temples and paintings preserve his battles and associations.

The Parthenon is a place whose front gables depict Athene’s birth and whose rear depicts her contest with Poseidon for Attica; its principal ivory-and-gold statue shows armed Athene with Victory, while its base depicts Pandora’s birth.

Athene is a goddess, widely worshipped in Athens and Attica and patron deity of Athens. In Libyan tradition she is associated with Poseidon and Tritonian Marsh as daughter, is represented with grey eyes, and is also portrayed springing from the head of Zeus. Her defining contest is with Poseidon for the soil of Attica: she displays and possesses the olive of Athene, which served as proof of her claim. Her most sacred statue stood on the Acropolis, formerly called the Polis; Athenians said it had fallen from heaven. Its temple held the sacred olive, ancient statues and offerings, and Callimachus’s golden lamp, which burned for a year when filled with oil. Her images and sanctuaries extend across many places. At Piraeus she appears armed with a spear beside Zeus; at Cnidus she is called Athene of the Fair Voyage. She has statues in the temple of Hephaestus, at Corinth, Titane, and elsewhere, including brazen works by Phidias and the Lemnian Athene. She is shown with Theseus and Hercules, her shield bears the battle of Theseus and the Amazons, and she is portrayed striking Marsyas after he took up flutes she had discarded. She is also called Athene the worker, Athene Area, Goddess of Horses, the Bridler, Injurious Athene, and Sthenias. Her cult includes temples, altars, and rites from Megara, Sparta, Phrixa, and Pontinus to Trœzen, Hermione, and Buporthmus. On the island once called Sphæria, Æthra built her a temple after a dream, and maidens of Trœzen dedicated maiden-girdles to Injurious Athene before marriage. As the Bridler, she aided Bellerophon, giving him Pegasus after breaking in and bridling him.

Zeus is a god worshipped through temples, altars, groves, sacrifices, priesthoods, festivals, statues, and votive offerings across Piraeus, Athens, Nemea, Ægina, Messenia, and Olympia. He is represented with varied titles and powers: Eleutherius, Counsellor, Guardian of the city, Milichian, Nemean, Pan-Hellenian, of Ithome, of the Market-Place, Supreme, Decider of Fate, and God of Oaths. His images bear such attributes as a sceptre, Victory, thunderbolts, eagles, javelins, lilies, and Ganymede; one Piraeus statue was gold and held a sceptre and Victory. Records connect him with Athene’s birth from his head; fatherhood of Zethus and Amphion; Ægina and Æacus; rain after drought; foreknowledge of human events; and transformations or deceptions involving a cuckoo and the appearance of Amphitryon. The account begins with his cult image at Piraeus and Athene’s birth, then moves through ancient altars, sacrifices, temples, and local traditions. It tells of Zeus producing settlers for Ægina, being reared by Ithome and Neda in Messenian tradition, and receiving extensive honor at Olympia. There, his temple, statue, altars, oath ritual, and numerous offerings culminate the record, showing him as a central recipient of public worship, civic guardianship, rain, prophecy, and formal oaths.
Victory is a monument on a pillar at Olympia, designed by Mendæan Pæonius and apparently made from enemy spoils; the Messenians said it commemorated their share with the Athenians at Sphacteria.

The Macedonians appear as a military and political group active across Greece. They believed Ptolemy was Philip’s son, turned hostile to Perdiccas after his failed Egyptian expedition, and considered sibling marriage unusual. After Chaeronea they controlled much of Greece, occupying Athens through garrisons at Munychia, the Piraeus, and the long walls; they also held Corinth, Salamis, Sunium, and the Museum until Olympiodorus expelled them from Athens. Their power was feared, though Aratus eventually allied with them, and Elis both supported them after Philip’s intervention and later joined opposition to Antipater and them after Alexander’s death. They supported Cassander and his sons, opposed Pyrrhus, and were defeated by him in Upper Macedonia. Under Demetrius, son of Philip, they attacked Messene but were driven out with heavy losses. Antigonus fortified towns during the Laconian war.

has_boundary_with Attica [at the Platæan district, formerly; later at Mount Cithæron] As one traveled from Eleusis toward Bœotia, the Platæan district marked the old boundary between the Athenians and the people of Eleutheræ. After Eleutheræ joined Athens, Mount Cithæron in Bœotia became the boundary.

Artemis is a deity associated with death in the story of Pirene’s transformation and with temples, cults, statues, images, and worship across Cenchreae, Corinth, Sicyon, Sparta, and Limnæum. Her representations include an old wooden statue, a hunting statue, a golden image, a brass statue with wings, leopard, and lion, and figures in civic and sacred decoration. She is honored under forms and titles including Limnæa, Pheræan, Orthian, Cnagian, and Leucophryene. Her images participate in procession, sacrifice, dance, and traditions of arrival from the Tauric Chersonese and Crete.

Demeter is a worshipped deity associated with temples, precincts, statues, rites, mysteries, and sacred communities across several places. In the Argive account, she appears as a woman and kills Pyrrhus by throwing a tile; an oracle leads to a temple being erected where he dies. Near the Nine Springs, traditions connect her with learning of Proserpine’s rape and with teaching Triptolemus, Eubules, and others to sow corn. She repays Phytalus’s hospitality with a fig tree, is honored with Proserpine, Athene, and Poseidon in the grove of Lacius, and is represented in a temple once dedicated to Apollo. The Rheti are sacred to her, and rites with Proserpine are performed by Celeus’s daughters; after the rape, she is said to sit disguised as an old woman at the Well of Flowers. Taking compassion on Plemnæus, she rears his son, prompting a temple. She has further worship at Phlius, where mysteries are celebrated, and at Hermione as Chthonia, as well as at Lerna and Didymi.

The Persians invade Attica, land at Marathon, and bring Parian marble to Rhamnus to prepare a victory trophy before conquering Athens. They are defeated at Marathon, driven into marshy ground and Marathon’s muddy lake, killed while boarding ships, and lose ships in retreat. Some also land at the Acropolis and kill Athenians behind wooden palisades. Spoil taken from them is used for Phidias’s brazen statue of Athene.

Aphrodite is a deity honored through temples, shrines, statues, offerings, and varied local forms. She is called Celestial Aphrodite on a square statue and appears in images by Praxiteles, Canachus, Hermogenes of Cythera, and others: seated in gold and ivory, wooden at Argos, stone near the sea, armed on Acrocorinth and at Sparta, and fettered in Sparta’s upper shrine. Her places of worship span Corinth, Acrocorinth, Sicyon, Argos, Hermione, Trœzen, Sparta, Epidaurus Limera, and Cænepolis. Corinthian tradition says she received Acrocorinth from the Sun; Polynices and associated Argives dedicated her Argive image. Her cult includes restricted rites at Sicyon, marriage-related sacrifices by maidens and widows at Hermione, and temples named Peeping, Bridal, of the Height, Marine, and of the Harbour. She encourages Jason in wooing Medea, while her fetters signify bonds of love between men and women. The records close with her notable temple at Epidaurus Limera and another near the sea at Cænepolis.

Hera is a goddess with temples and statues at Phlius, Cleonæ, near Mycenæ, on Pron, at Sparta, and at Olympia. Her chief recorded sanctuary near Mycenæ holds Polycletus’s gold-and-ivory seated statue, with a pomegranate and temple traditions about her nurses, marriage with Zeus, cuckoo, peacock, and an older temple burned after Chryseis’s lamp caught fire. She receives goat sacrifices at Sparta; at Olympia, sixteen matrons weave her a shawl and hold games every fifth year.

Antiope, Nycteus’s daughter and reputedly linked to Asopus, was renowned for beauty. Taken or sought in marriage by Epopeus, she was taken to Thebes, bore Zethus and Amphion near Eleutheræ, and became a statue at Aphrodite’s Sicyon temple.
The Amazons fought Hercules at Themiscyra, then Athens after their army’s destruction, were defeated by Theseus, and are depicted fighting Athenians before later fighting at Ilium and other Greeks.

Hercules is a Greek hero whose identity is also treated as divine: at Sicyon he received sacrifice first as a hero and later as a god, while the Thasians called him a god. His importance lies in the many feats, conflicts, Labours, cults, statues, temples, games, and artistic representations attached to him across Greece. Tradition begins with him throttling snakes, then attributes to him the defeat of the Nemean lion, the shooting of the hydra, and arrows dipped in the hydra’s gall. He released Prometheus after killing the eagle tormenting him, bore or offered to bear Atlas’s burden, fought Geryon, Centaurs, Amazons, and at Pylos, where Athene cooperated with him and Pluto opposed him; he also killed the robber Saurus and destroyed Pylos. After killing Iphitus, he fought Hippocoon and his sons because they would not clear him of guilt and because Œonus was killed. Returning with allies, he defeated them and founded temples to Athene the Exactor of due punishment and Hera Goateater. He defeated the Dryopes and captured their town, cleared Augeas’s land by diverting the Menius, and, after being denied payment, captured and sacked Elis with Argive, Theban, and Arcadian assistance. At Olympia he is linked to an altar and the title Assistant, victories in wrestling and the pancratium, sacrifices to Zeus, the introduction of white poplar, and reliefs of his Labours. He was represented in paintings, on the chest of Cypselus, in votive offerings, and in statues holding club and bow or armed. Traditions place Cerberus’s emergence through a hole at Clymenus’ place, and associate him with temples and images at Sparta, Sicyon, Elis, Thasos, and elsewhere. He also appears as Timosthenes in connection with a Thasian priesthood.
is_a great light of Tragedy Euripides was regarded as one of the great lights of Tragedy. His statue stood among those of tragic and comic dramatists in the theatre.

Æschylus, a great light of Tragedy, fought at Marathon and wrote tragedy after a dream command from Dionysus; he represented Erinnyes with snakes, described seven warriors, and received a statue long after death.
Hiero, Gelon’s brother, becomes tyrant of Syracuse, wins Olympian contests, and is commemorated by offerings made by his son Dinomenes.
Homer, who wrote the Iliad, is cited for accounts of Mecisteus, Cyllene, Achilles’ journey to Troy, Hades traditions, Cardamyle, and Enope.

Praxiteles created or was credited with the Satyr and Cupid and designed the Brauronian Artemis statue; he especially prized the Satyr and Cupid, reportedly revealing them as his finest works to Phryne.

Poseidon is a deity associated with water, sea-facing lands, and powerful contests over territory. He is shown bringing forth water and leaving a trident mark in rock during his contest with Athene for Attica; he loses Argos to Hera’s arbitrators, floods the region, and later withdraws the water after Hera’s intervention. Briareus awards him the Isthmus and land toward the sea in a dispute with the Sun. His anger also threatens Trœzen with barrenness through brine, but sacrifices and prayers mollify him. He is linked by parentage or consort to Amphitrite, Palemon, Peratus, Athene, Cercyon, and Æthra, and is represented carrying off Taygetes. His importance is expressed through widespread worship: groves, temples, sanctuaries, altars, statues, and representations occur at Colonus, Corinth, Calaurea, Tænarum, Olympia, Sparta, and elsewhere. Images show him with a dolphin, while local traditions preserve his territorial claims, punishments, reconciliations, and honors.

Dionysus is a god honored through temples, shrines, statues, altars, processions, and festivals. The people of Brasiæ said he arrived there as an infant in a chest with Semele, was reared there, and was nursed by Ino in a cave; the nearby plain was called his garden. He was said to descend to Hades to fetch Semele, to take the drunken Hephæstus to Heaven, and to carry off Ariadne after Theseus abandoned her. At Argos he was said to have warred with Perseus, later become friendly with him, and receive great honors. Narcæus and Physcoa were said to be his first worshippers. His cult included the oldest temple at the theatre, temples at Eleutheræ, Sicyon, the Hollow Way, Argos, Las, and elsewhere; images by Eleuthereus, Alcamenes, and Praxiteles; Bacchantes; and a yearly torchlit procession at Sicyon. Elis honored him above every other god and said he frequented the Thyia festival.

Apollo is a deity represented, worshipped, and honoured across many places through temples, sanctuaries, statues, epithets, an oracle, and local traditions. A brazen statue outside the Parthenon, said to be by Phidias, calls him Apollo Averter of Locusts because he removed locusts that devastated the land. At Megara he was said to help Alcathous build the wall and to leave his harp on a stone which sounds like a harp when struck; the city also had several temples and forms of Apollo. He appears in Corinth, Tenea, Sicyon, Hermione, Didymi, Coccygium, Sparta, Amyclæ, Gythium, Epidelium, Zarax, Pyrrhichus, Las, and near Corone. His titles include Lycian or Wolf-god, Pythæan, Apollo of the Borders, Corydus, Carnean, Amazonius, Clarian, Pythius, Decataphorus, Archegetes, Protecting, Carinus, Latoan, and Averter of Locusts. At Sicyon he was credited with curing the daughters of Prœtus and destroying wolves. At Amyclæ women annually wove him a coat, and his large ancient statue stood on a base associated with Hyacinthus, whom he loved; he was worshipped there with Dionysus. Near Corone, his highly honoured and reputedly most ancient temple held a wooden statue and a brazen dedication said to be from the Argonauts, and the Messenians believed Corydus healed diseases. Other records present him as leading the Muses in song, victorious in racing and boxing at Olympia, taking Marpessa, and having amour with Creusa. His oracle of the Ridgeway was still functioning in the author’s time.

is_named_after Ceramus [the hero reputed to be its ancestor] Ceramicus took its name from the hero Ceramus, who was reputed to be the son of Dionysus and Ariadne. Its area included the royal portico, paintings, temples, the council chamber, and the Rotunda.
Artaxerxes, son of Darius and Persian king, responded to Agesilaus’s victories by executing Tissaphernes and funding Timocrates to provoke war against the Lacedæmonians.

Salamis lies opposite Eleusis and extends toward Megaris. It contains market ruins, an ebony statue and temple of Ajax, temples of Artemis and Cychreus, and a trophy commemorating Themistocles’ naval victory for the Greeks.

The Lacedæmonians are a Dorian, Spartan people whose city is Sparta. They maintained two royal houses, followed the laws associated with Lycurgus, preserved temples, monuments, and traditions, and at times received kings’ bodies and buried Agesilaus with unmatched honours. Their history is dominated by warfare, expansion, changing alliances, and later reversals. They established Sparta and expanded against neighboring peoples. In the wars with Messenia, they secretly prepared, swore not to end the war before winning, and captured Amphea in a night attack. After raids, battles, defeat, renewed war, and the capture of Ithome, they imposed tribute and mourning obligations on the Messenians. In the later struggle they fought Aristomenes, bribed Aristocrates before the Great Trench, besieged Eira for eleven years with Corinthian and Cretan support, captured it, incorporated captives among the Helots, conquered and divided Messenia, and granted Mothone to the people of Nauplia. They also fought widely in Argolis, Elis, Bœotia, Athens, and elsewhere. Under Nicander they invaded Argolis with Asine; they later held Thyrea briefly, but Philip son of Amyntas confined them to their original boundaries. They delayed at Marathon by custom, defeated Athenians at Tanagra, were routed at Leuctra, and suffered defeat at Sellasia. They supported Athenians, fought or intervened in conflicts involving Thebes, Elis, Argos, and Messenia, and bred horses with exceptional attention after the invasion of the Medes. Their power was repeatedly challenged: Pyrrhus nearly took Sparta despite Argive and Messenian allies; Antigonus and the Achæans captured Sparta; and, after Cleomenes’s reign, they adopted a republican government. Yet they recovered their old polity after the capture, retained Sparta, and later had friendly relations with the Messenians when those people aided them against Pyrrhus.

Xenophon, son of Gryllus, was exiled from Athens for joining Cyrus against the Persian king, received Scillus from the Lacedæmonians, built a temple and grove there to Ephesian Artemis, and was reportedly acquitted over accepting Scillus.

Epaminondas, son of Cleommis, restores the Messenians’ country and cities after the Theban victory at Leuctra, prompted by a dream. He consults Epiteles, recovers the Messenian Mysteries, chooses and builds Messene as a base against the Lacedæmonians, and secures Aristomenes’ shield before Leuctra. He is later honored with statues at Messene.

The Galati, called Celts, came from remotest Europe, overran Illyria, Macedonia and Thessaly, and invaded Greece. Defeated near Delphi by local forces amid storms and falling rocks, many crossed into Asia Minor; others died on a Nile desert island by swords and famine.

are_called Galati [in later usage] The people later called Galati were originally called Celts by themselves and by other nations. Their army invaded Greece, reached Thermopylæ, and sought to plunder the treasures at Delphi before being driven back.

Thermopylæ is a narrow pass defended by Leonidas and 300 Lacedæmonians against Xerxes’ army. Greek volunteers under Callippus tried to block the Galati, but they used Ephialtes’ route, routed the Phocians, entered Greece, and Athenians suffered near the Lamiac Gulf; Hydarnes likewise flanked Leonidas’ position.
The Phocians seize Apollo’s temple at Delphi, gain mercenary aid and public support, and plan to kill young men, enslave women and children, and destroy the city, until Archidamus prevents them.

Delphi is a sanctuary and city centered on its renowned oracle and priestess, repeatedly consulted by communities and rulers for guidance on wars, succession, restoration, fines, famine, and political disputes. It directs the Athenians to pay Callippus’ fine, restrains Hercules from attacking Pisa, calls Iphitus to restore the Olympian games, and gives messages to the Thasians. Its pronouncements shape accounts of the Dorians, Aristodemus’ sons, Orestes’ bones, Demaratus, Lacedæmonian and Messenian conflict, and Aletes. Yet its authority is vulnerable: Cleomenes bribes its priestess, and the Phocians seize Apollo’s temple and contemplate destroying the city before Archidamus prevents it. Finally, the Galati advance to plunder its treasures, but Delphians, Phocians, and Ætolians resist and win; the Delphians then sacrifice to Pyrrhus.

l: Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, Description of Greece
s: Pyrrhus of Epirus is a king of Epirus who returned from exile with Egyptian aid from Ptolemy I Soter. After fighting in Corcyra, Macedonia, and against Lysimachus, he crossed from Greece into Italy at Tarentum’s invitation to fight Rome, then led a Sicilian campaign after Syracuse invited him.

Achilles is a hero remembered in combat, fighting Memnon while their mothers watch. He is linked to Leuce, where a temple and statue stood and Leonymus reported seeing him with companions. Cults honored him near Sparta and at Elis, where he had a cenotaph. Though associated with Helen’s marriage quest, the account denies he was her suitor or bound by Tyndareus’ oath.

Asia Minor was invaded by the Lacedæmonians under Agesilaus in an attempt to attack Persia. Agesilaus won a major victory over Tissaphernes there before the Corinthian War forced him to return to Greece.

Antiochus, son of Phintas, ruled Messenia with Androcles, opposed surrendering Polychares and urged arbitration, became sole king after Androcles' death, dedicated a veil at Olympia, and died before open war.

has_temple_at Salamis [with an ebony statue] Ajax was associated with Salamis, where he had a temple and an ebony statue, and the Athenians paid divine honours to him and to Eurysaces. A stone near the harbour was shown as the place where Telamon sat watching Ajax’s sons sail to Aulis, and the people of Salamis said that a distinctive white-and-red flower first appeared on the island after Ajax’s death.

Eumolpus, a noble man in Homer’s poem, was said to come from Thrace as the son of Poseidon and Chione. He was killed in the Eleusinian-Athenian battle after his son Immaradus died; Athenians and Euboeans showed his tomb.

was_buried_in Megara [his tomb was proof of Athenian possession] Pandion was said to have received Megaris from its king Pylas, and his tomb was shown in that district. His son Nisus became king of Megara, and Pandion also had a hero-chapel and divine honors at Megara.

Megara is a place originally said to have belonged to the Athenians through a bequest to Pandion by Pylas, though evidence also numbered it among Athenians. When Codrus was king, Peloponnesians took it and gave it to Corinthians and other allies; after capture and resettlement, its inhabitants became Dorians in customs and dialect. Its name is attributed to Megareus in one tradition. After Hyperion’s death it replaced kingship with annually chosen chief magistrates. It contains Alcathous’s citadel, temples, tombs, hero-chapels, Nisæa, Pagæ, Ægosthena, and roads toward Corinth.

Attalus, a king, son of Attalus and nephew of Philetærus, received the kingdom from his cousin Eumenes. His greatest achievement was driving the Galatians from the coast into inland Galatia. He also made portrayals of giants, Amazons, Marathon, and Galati, and created the Lycian Apollo; his exploits later lacked adequate record.

Emperor Adrian is presented as a benefactor, especially to Athens and the peoples he ruled. Honoured there with a statue, he built and adorned temples, including Apollo’s old white-stone temple. He avoided war except to punish the Hebrews’ revolt, and inscriptions recorded his gifts and benefactions.

shook Greece [to its foundation] The Peloponnesian War left Athens weakened, and the Athenians cited the strain of the war and the city’s recovery from the plague when declining to aid Agesilaus’ expedition to Asia.

l: battle of Leuctra, Description of Greece
s: The battle of Leuctra was won by the Thebans, with Aristomenes’ shield displayed as a trophy. Their victory reversed Lacedæmonian fortune, aided the restoration of the Messenians, prompted the recall of exiles, and was later commemorated by returning the shield as a votive offering.

l: Celtic invasion of Greece, Description of Greece
s: is_a invasion [conducted by the Galati] The Celtic invasion brought an army through Illyria, Macedonia, and Thessaly to Thermopylæ. The invaders forced the pass by the route used by Ephialtes and then advanced toward Delphi, where Greek forces defeated them; many survivors crossed into Asia Minor and established themselves in the region later called Galatia.

Philip, son of Amyntas, was a king who took control after Antigonus and sought to dominate Greece. He captured most Greek cities, reduced Greece while it was weakened after the Peloponnesian War, and weakened Athens by taking its islands and ending its naval supremacy. Elis joined the Macedonians and later aided his attack on the Lacedæmonians. He married Eurydice and had children, including Demetrius; an account calls Ptolemy his son by Berenice. Violent toward subjects, he poisoned Aratus, Euryclides, and Micon. Athens later honored him with gifts and statues. He died from sorrow after Demetrius was poisoned by Perseus.

Alexander, son of Philip son of Amyntas, was a king who ruled the Macedonian empire after Philip. Aided by Ptolemy in danger at Oxydracæ, he conquered Porus and India and brought elephants to Europe. After his death, his dominions split; buried at Memphis, his corpse was later brought away by Ptolemy I Soter.

Cleomenes is presented as a Spartan king of the Agid royal house, variously named son of Anaxandrides or Leonidas. He removed Eurydamidas by poison, weakened or abolished the Ephors and Senate in favor of the Great Council of Patronomi, and manipulated a Delphic priestess to depose Demaratus. He fought Argives and Achæans, captured Megalopolis during a truce, and was credited with actions in Athens and Ægina. Defeated by Antigonus and the Achæans at Sellasia, he fled to Egypt, escaped prison, stirred trouble in Alexandria, and died by self-inflicted violence in madness.
Perdiccas opposed Ptolemy while attempting to take Egypt, led Aridæus and the young Alexander, was driven out, lost support, and was assassinated by his Macedonian bodyguard.

Seleucus, son of Antiochus and a king described as upright, pious, and religious, was exiled by Antigonus and welcomed by Ptolemy. Ptolemy rallied Cassander and Lysimachus against Antigonus. Seleucus restored a brazen Apollo and made conditions with Ptolemy; later refugees were received after Antiochus violated them.

Demetrius, son of Antigonus, was a boy in years but a man in intellect, a military commander and ruler who deposed an Athenian ruler, fortified Museum, governed Syria and Phœnicia, won victories in Cyprus, and besieged Rhodes unsuccessfully. After succeeding Antigonus, he faced Lysimachus, crossed into Asia Minor, and was captured by Seleucus.
Cassander rules Macedonia dependent on Antigonus, maintains friendship with Lysimachus, opposes Æacides, and campaigns against young Pyrrhus.

Lysimachus, a Macedonian and Alexander the Great’s armour-bearer, ruled Thrace after Alexander’s death, fought several rivals, and eventually ruled Macedonia. Though father of Agathocles and husband of Arsinoe, he permitted Agathocles’ execution, then was defeated and killed by Seleucus I.

Menelaus pursues Helen to kill her during Ilium’s sack, returns after its capture to place statues near Aphrodite Migonitis, dies, and is said by the Lacedæmonians to be buried with Helen at Therapne.

l: Magas of Cyrene, Description of Greece
s: Magas, Berenice’s son and Ptolemy I Soter’s uterine brother, governed Cyrene, led its revolt and march toward Egypt, turned back amid a Marmaridæ revolt, and persuaded Antiochus I to attack Egypt.

Pyrrhus is a king of Epirus and Thesprotia, identified as the son of Achilles and grandson of Æacus. He was associated with a voyage from Scyrus to Sparta to marry Hermione, during which he was said to name the river Scyras; he was also linked to Pyrrhichus. After withdrawing from Italy by circulating a report of expected aid, he fought Antigonus, whose failure to send Italian reinforcements was given as the cause of their war. Pyrrhus defeated Antigonus’s forces, gained Upper Macedonia and Thessaly, and entered the Peloponnese at Cleonymus’s invitation. He invaded Sparta and nearly captured it, then died fighting at Argos. His body was burned there; his bones and shield were associated with Demeter’s temple, and he had a statue in the Altis.

Ptolemy entered Egypt, killed Cleomenes, secured the country with garrisons, and defended it against Perdiccas, Antigonus, and Demetrius. Egypt was protected at Pelusium by land forces and by a fleet guarding the river. Egypt was threatened by Magas of Cyrene and Antiochus I, but Ptolemy I Soter defended it by guarding the approaches, using troops, and sending forces to ravage Antiochus’s territory. A group of 4,000 Galati mercenaries sent to a desert island in the Nile perished there.

revolted_against Ptolemy I Soter [under the leadership of Magas] Cyrene revolted from Ptolemy I Soter after Magas persuaded its people to support him. Magas marched with an army from Cyrene toward Egypt but turned back when the Marmaridæ rebelled.
Ptolemy seized Syria after the death of Perdiccas, but Antigonus later took it by surprise and handed it over to Demetrius. After Antigonus’s death, Ptolemy took Syria again.
Ptolemy seized Phœnicia together with Syria after the death of Perdiccas. Antigonus later captured it and placed it under Demetrius, and Ptolemy subsequently recovered it after Antigonus’s death.

Rhodes was the home of Diagoras and his family, including Dorieus. Dorieus and Pisirodus were entered as Thurians after faction drove them from Rhodes, although Dorieus later returned; Rhodes was also persuaded by Conon to revolt from the Lacedæmonians and join the Athenians and the great king.

l: government of Egypt and of the Mysi, Description of Greece
s: The unit proposes to explain how the government of Egypt and of the Mysi, along with that of neighboring nations, came to the fathers of Ptolemy and Attalus.

l: kingdom of Egypt, Description of Greece
s: Perdiccas plotted to take the kingdom of Egypt from Ptolemy but was driven out. Ptolemy preserved the kingdom when Antigonus and Demetrius attacked it.
After the death of Alexander, Ptolemy was chiefly responsible for having the different nationalities divided into kingdoms.

l: war against Antigonus, Description of Greece
s: Ptolemy persuaded Cassander and Lysimachus to join him in war against Antigonus, presenting the exile of Seleucus and Antigonus’s aggrandizement as a common danger. The conflict included fighting in Syria, Phœnicia, Cyprus, Egypt, and Rhodes, and ended with Antigonus losing most of his forces and dying.

l: siege of Egypt, Description of Greece
s: Antigonus and Demetrius blockaded Egypt by land and sea after Ptolemy fled there. Ptolemy maintained his position at Pelusium with an army and used his fleet to keep the enemy from the river, preventing the capture of Egypt.

l: death of Alexander, Description of Greece
s: After the death of Alexander, Ptolemy resisted giving all of Alexander’s dominions to Aridæus and helped divide the empire into separate kingdoms. Alexander’s body was diverted from its intended burial at Ægæ and buried by Ptolemy at Memphis.

l: assassination of Perdiccas, Description of Greece
s: Perdiccas was assassinated by his bodyguard after his failed attempt to take Egypt from Ptolemy left him without his former prestige and unpopular among the Macedonians.

l: power of Antigonus, Description of Greece
s: The power of Antigonus was opposed by Ptolemy, Cassander, Lysimachus, and Seleucus. Antigonus eventually fought their combined forces, lost most of his army, and died, bringing about the defeat of his power.
Antiochus I, son of Seleucus I, was persuaded by Magas to plan invading Egypt but was stopped by Ptolemy’s raids and resistance.
Antigonus I and the Macedonians opposed the Athenians, against whom Ptolemy I Soter sent a fleet. Lysimachus later destroyed Antigonus I’s rule in Asia Minor.
Philetærus, a Paphlagonian eunuch and Docimus’s nephew, controlled Lysimachus’s money, revolted and invited Seleucus I, then occupied Pergamum and offered himself and the money to Seleucus.

Amphiaraus is a figure worshipped as a god at Oropus, where he has a temple, a white-stone statue, and an oracle giving direction through dreams. During the rout from Thebes, the earth swallowed him, his chariot, and Bato, reportedly at Harma rather than Oropus. After becoming a god, he instituted dream divination for worshippers who sacrifice and sleep in a ram’s skin.

leads_army_into Greece [during Leonidas’ reign] Xerxes led the Persian army into Greece during Leonidas’ reign. The text calls him the most sagacious and renowned of the kings of the Medes and Persians and says his advance was checked at Thermopylæ until the Greek flank was exposed.

Demosthenes was twice exiled by the Athenians, first to Calauria and again after the defeat at Lamia. Returning to Calauria, he died by poison, avoiding surrender by Archias to Antipater and the Macedonians. He was honored with a tomb in Poseidon’s precinct and elsewhere in Greece, and Philoxenus’ letters omitted him from recipients of Harpalus’ money.

Trœzen is a proud country with a remembered line of kings from Orus to Pittheus. Its people preserve temples, altars, monuments, sanctuaries, landmarks, and traditions for Artemis, Apollo, the Muses, Orestes, Hippolytus, Theseus, Athene, Poseidon, Aphrodite, Pan, Isis, Demeter, and others. Its customs unfold through yearly sacrifices, maidens’ offerings, Stonethrowing, Saronia, and routes through its surrounding district.
Alcamenes, son of Teleclus and king of the Lacedæmonians, made Hecate with three heads and bodies and led the night attack capturing Amphea.

l: Ptolemy II Philadelphus, Description of Greece
s: Ptolemy II Philadelphus is an Egyptian king represented by statues in the Athenian Odeum and among the Athenian Eponymi, near his sister Arsinoe.

l: Ptolemy VI Philometor, Description of Greece
s: Ptolemy VI Philometor, an eighth-generation descendant of Ptolemy I Soter and eldest son of Cleopatra I, was hated by her, banished to Cyprus, returned after Alexander fled and Cleopatra I was killed, regained Egypt, suppressed the Theban revolt, and received an Athenian bronze statue with Berenice.
Cleopatra I, mother of Ptolemy VI Philometor and Alexander, opposed her eldest son's succession, promoted Alexander through a fabricated plot, and was eventually killed by him.

l: Alexander (brother of Ptolemy VI), Description of Greece
s: was_younger_brother_of Ptolemy VI Philometor Alexander, the younger brother of Ptolemy VI Philometor, was sent to Cyprus by Cleopatra I and later became king when Philometor fled. He killed Cleopatra after she had helped secure his accession, then fled when the crime was discovered, allowing Philometor to return.

Thebes is a place bounded by Asopus on the side of Platæa. It was ruled by Lycus for Labdacus and by Creon for Laodamas. It sent an army against Epopeus over Antiope; under Creon, a burial dispute led to conflict with Athens and Bœotia. It later defended Haliartus against Lysander and the Lacedæmonians, compelled Pausanias to make a treaty, revolted against Ptolemy VI Philometor, and was severely punished after submission.
Agathocles, son of Lysimachus, was captured by the Getæ campaigning against Dromichetes, had children with Lysandra, and was killed through Arsinoe’s conspiracy.

l: Arsinoe (wife of Lysimachus), Description of Greece
s: Arsinoe, wife of Lysimachus and sister of Lysandra, conspired against Agathocles, reportedly fearing for her children’s future after Lysimachus’s death; another account attributes the plot to rejected love.

contains Nestus [in its mountainous part] Lysimachus ruled the part of Thrace adjoining Macedonia after Alexander the Great’s death. The text says that Thrace was densely populated and later became subject to the Romans.

Epirus, Pyrrhus’s homeland, was ruled by his descendants amid succession struggles involving Æacides, Alcetas, and Pyrrhus; Lysimachus ravaged it, and Pyrrhus’s death, after he entered the Peloponnese and did not return, ended its glory.

Romans are a group defined here by successive wars and conquests. They first fought Pyrrhus in Italy, initially confused by his arrival and elephants, then opposed his departure despite allowing him to reach the Ceraunian Mountains. Later, supported by Athenians, they defeated Aristion, Mithridates’ generals, captured Athens, and besieged the Piræus. They conquered the Greeks after the Achaean revolt, destroyed Corinth under Mummius, and later drove Mithridates about after destroying his power.

Tarentum, at war with the Romans and unable to resist alone, invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, citing prior naval aid against Corcyra. After defeat in Italy, Pyrrhus sailed there with his remaining fleet and summoned its chief men, promising aid.

After Pyrrhus suffered a defeat in Italy, he escaped by crossing toward the Ceraunian Mountains under cover of night. The failure to receive reinforcements for the war in Italy became one of his main charges against Antigonus.

Syracuse, the only Sicilian Greek city remaining, was besieged by Carthaginians; it invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, who raised the siege; it was ruled by Hiero son of Dinomenes then Hiero son of Hierocles, after whose assassination Dinomenes tried to kill Hippocrates.
Originally Tyrians and Phoenicians, the Carthaginians were the greatest barbarian maritime nation, repeatedly capturing Greek cities in Sicily until Pyrrhus challenged their naval power.

l: Romans’ war with Pyrrhus, Description of Greece
s: The Romans’ war with Pyrrhus began after Tarentum invited him to intervene. Pyrrhus crossed into Italy unexpectedly, attacked the Romans when they were attacking Tarentum, and used elephants to cause panic.

l: Pyrrhus’s Italian campaign, Description of Greece
s: During Pyrrhus’s Italian campaign, he transported cavalry, infantry, and elephants from Greece to aid Tarentum and other Italians against Rome. His unexpected arrival initially confused the Romans.

l: Pyrrhus’s Sicilian campaign, Description of Greece
s: During Pyrrhus’s Sicilian campaign, he answered an embassy from Syracuse, crossed from Tarentum, and compelled the Carthaginians to raise their siege. He then became overconfident and sought to fight the Carthaginians at sea.

resulted_from war with Seleucus I [after defeat in Asia Minor] Lysimachus’s death occurred after he crossed into Asia Minor and fought Seleucus I. He was badly defeated and killed, while his son Alexander later recovered the corpse and buried it in the Thracian Chersonese between Cardia and Pactye.
Sicily became the destination of the Messenian exiles after Anaxilas invited them to settle in Zancle. The Messenians conquered the city and established their new community there.

Larissa is the citadel of Argos, named in Argive tradition after the daughter of Pelasgus and associated with two Thessalian cities of the same name. Approaching it are temples of Hera Dwelling on the Heights and Apollo of the Ridgeway, a race-course for games to Nemean Zeus and Hera, and a monument to the sons of Ægyptus. On its summit stands the roofless temple of Larissæan Zeus; it also contains temples, offerings, and Athene’s temple with Priam’s wooden three-eyed Zeus.

Cleonymus, a Lacedæmonian of the royal house and son of Cleomenes, disputed Sparta’s kingship with Areus but was excluded when the Senate chose Areus. Resentful, he persuaded Pyrrhus to enter the Peloponnese and Sparta to seek the kingdom, harming his country and razing Zarax.

The Peloponnese is a place divided into five parts, including Arcadia, Achaia, and three Dorian regions; Arcadians and Achæans are indigenous, while others arrived from elsewhere. The Heraclidæ returned under Tisamenus, claiming Argos and Messenia and displacing earlier rulers. After Ithome fell, Messenians evacuated, were scattered, and were later recalled and restored. It later received Demetrius’s fleet expedition and Pyrrhus, who ravaged Lacedæmonian territory, nearly took Sparta, and reached Argos.

was_friendly_to Athenians [despite maintaining peace between the Peloponnesians and Athenians] Platæa was friendly to the Athenians and had tried to preserve peace between the Athenians and Peloponnesians. Archidamus captured it after a siege despite its lack of responsibility for the conflict.
Spartan king who succeeded Agesipolis, led the Lacedæmonians against the Bœotians at Leuctra, and was killed early in battle.

The Thebans refused to join Agesilaus’ invasion of Asia, opposed the Lacedæmonians, and were defeated at Coronea after the dispute involving Locrians and Phocians. After Leuctra, they recalled exiled Messenians and, with Epaminondas, helped establish the restored Messenian capital, deterring Lacedæmonian interference.

Leuctra, about twenty stades from Pephnos, is a place whose name has no known explanation. It has temples or statues of Æsculapius, Ino, Cassandra, Carnean Apollo, Athene, Eros, and Ithomatan Zeus; Eros has a winter-flowing grove, and Zeus was found after a fire. It was the site of a Theban victory that led to disaster for the Lacedæmonians and restoration of the Messenians.
Agesipolis, king of Sparta and son of Pausanias’ royal successor, came of age, invaded Argos but withdrew after disasters, then campaigned successfully in Chalcidice and died suddenly near Olynthus.

Areus, son of Acrotatus, was chosen king of the Lacedæmonians instead of Cleonymus. He led them in support of Athens against Antigonus, but withdrew when provisions were consumed. Olympia had statues of him, including one on horseback and one dedicated by the men of Elis.

Leonidas is presented as a king of Sparta and of the Lacedæmonians, succeeding Cleomenes because he was the only surviving male of Eurysthenes’ family. He commanded 300 Lacedæmonians at Thermopylæ and died resisting Xerxes’ invasion. Charges by Lysander and Cleombrotus led to his deposition and exile in Arcadia, after which he was recalled to kingship. Forty years after his death, Pausanias moved his remains to Sparta, where his tomb hosts annual Spartan speeches and a contest.
Sphacteria is an island before the harbour of Pylos. Lacedæmonian reverses there made it world-famous; Athenians captured shields on it and commemorated their success with a brazen Victory statue.

Argos is a city in the Peloponnese, named after Argos, the daughter’s son of Phoroneus. It became the kingdom of Acrisius after the division by the sons of Abas; Perseus later exchanged it with Megapenthes after killing Acrisius. Its kingdom was divided among three royal lines before Orestes acquired it with Sparta, and the Heraclidæ expelled Tisamenus. Argos later figured in conflict with the Lacedæmonians over Cynuria and in invasions by Cleomenes and Agesipolis. Cleomenes’ defeat of the Argives left it nearly without men, but Telesilla organized its defense. Under Aristomachus, Aratus helped establish democracy and bring Argos into the Achæan league. Pyrrhus entered while pursuing fugitives, and dispersed fighting followed in its temples, houses, and alleys. The city and its roads to Tegea, Mantinea, Lyrceia, Orneæ, Epidaurus, and Mycenæ are marked by temples, tombs, monuments, ruins, sacred places, and Argive traditions.

Messene was the Messenians’ homeland, under Ithome and about 80 stades from the mouth of the Pamisus. During the siege of Eira it was defeated at the Great Trench; Theoclus read the oracle as ending its safety, and Aristomenes hid its sacred records for a hoped-for recovery. After Eira fell, it could not be recovered, and its name was given to former Zancle in Sicily. Later Messene repelled Demetrius’ Macedonians, received Arcadians from Megalopolis with equal rights, resisted Nabis, and rejoined the Achæan League. It had a stone circular wall, towers and battlements, and a nearby temple of Serapis and Isis.

Sparta, also called Lacedæmon, is a city of the Lacedæmonians. Lacedæmon gave his name to the country and named the city Sparta after his wife; later accounts say Sparta was originally the city’s name, while Lacedæmon had named the whole district and then the city. It had two royal houses descended from the twin sons of Aristodemus. The city is defined by its civic, sacred, and martial landscape: a handsome market-place, public buildings, a theatre, royal tombs, monuments, temples, hero-chapels, statues, sacred precincts, fountains, groves, and the Dromus and Platanistas, where young men ran and fought under established customs. Its highest hill was called the citadel, though it lacked a notably high citadel. Its roads led toward Amyclæ, Therapne, Arcadia, and Gythium, and its territory included landmarks and routes around Caryæ, Sellasia, Thornax, and Scias. It had temples of Serapis and Olympian Zeus, and customs of honoring Enyalius in fetters, sacrificing goats to Hera, and entering battle to flutes, lyre, and harp.
