Sparta exercised authority beyond the city, receiving half the produce of Messenia and controlling coastal cities; it also became authority over Cardamyle. Yet Augustus liberated the Eleutherolacones from the yoke imposed by Sparta. In conflicts with the Messenians, Sparta withheld redress, prepared secretly for war, faced raids, scarcity, and riots, and escaped Aristomenes’ planned capture after warning reached Anaxander. A prophecy later foretold Sparta’s loss of its glorious flower when Messene was rebuilt, after which it resumed hostilities. Its government changed repeatedly. Cleomenes sought autocratic power and attacked the Achæans; after defeat and flight to Egypt, Sparta abandoned kingship for a republican form. Orestes later ruled as king at the Lacedæmonians’ request. Pyrrhus nearly took Sparta, prompting trenches and palisades, but the city prepared a defense. Finally, after Cleomenes’ defeat at Sellasia, Sparta was taken with Messenian, Aratus’, and Achæan help, and later faced Machanidas and Nabis.

Argives are a Greek people defined in these records by distinctive political traditions, extensive sacred memory, and recurrent warfare, especially with the Lacedæmonians. They said their people had uniquely been divided into three kingdoms, preserved accounts of royal succession, the Heraclidæ’s return, and Mysius’s hospitality to Demeter, and credited Phoroneus rather than Prometheus with fire. Seeking equality and home rule, they progressively curtailed their kings: Medon’s line retained only the title, and Meltas was deprived of the kingdom. Their city maintained many temples, tombs, statues, and memorials. Their traditions included Atheras and Mysius receiving Demeter, annual torch rites for Hypermnestra and Lynceus, and claims concerning heroes, the Palladium, and tombs, some claims disputed by the narrator. Survivors of the shipwreck at Caphareus, cold and hungry, prayed for rescue, found Dionysus’s cave, ate goats and wore their skins, then brought its statue home for continuing worship. Conflict shapes much of their history. They defeated the Lacedæmonians near Hysiæ, commemorated the victors, resisted Cleomenes through Telesilla and Argive women, and repeatedly contested Thyrea. They destroyed Asine after its people aided Lacedæmonian ravaging, while preserving Apollo’s temple there and burying Lysistratus nearby. They also dispossessed Orneæ and Tiryns, supported Deiphontes in Epidauria, aided Helos, and secretly and openly supported Messenians, including in the restoration of Messene. Later they became friendly with Athenians, allied with Mantineans and Athenians against the Lacedæmonians, and were said to dispute antiquity with Athenians more than other Greeks.

l: oracle at Delphi, Description of Greece
s: The oracle at Delphi, delivered by the Pythian Priestess, gives warnings and directions on war, succession, legitimacy, leadership, and religious restoration. It warns against a lame king and tells the Lacedæmonians about Aristodemus’ sons, Orestes’ bones, Messenian land, and Spartan ambushes; its answer on Demaratus’ legitimacy is compromised by bribery. It directs the Dorians to choose Oxylus and Iphitus to restore the Olympian games, while an earlier oracle protects Pisa.

l: war in Italy, Description of Greece
s: ends_with Pyrrhus [after Pyrrhus’s reverse and withdrawal] The war in Italy ended with Pyrrhus’s defeat and his flight from the country. His failure to receive reinforcements for this war was the principal reason he later declared war against Antigonus.

l: battle of Pyrrhus against Antigonus, Description of Greece
s: results_in Pyrrhus [victorious] In the battle against Antigonus, Pyrrhus defeated Antigonus’s own troops and the foreign Galatian contingent accompanying them. The victory gave him Upper Macedonia and Thessaly, and the captured Galatian and Macedonian arms were dedicated in temples.

l: death of Pyrrhus, Description of Greece
s: occurs_at Argos [during urban fighting] Pyrrhus died during the fighting in Argos after he entered the city while pursuing fugitives. The account says that a woman threw the fatal tile, while the Argives attributed the act to Demeter appearing as a woman.

l: glory of Epirus, Description of Greece
s: ends_with death of Pyrrhus [at Pyrrhus’s death] The glory of Epirus ended with the death of Pyrrhus. His death is compared with the supernatural ends attributed to other members of the line of the Æacidæ.

Athens is a place marked by ancient rule, religious monuments, civic acts, conflict, loss, and recovery. After Thymœtes was driven out, Melanthus ruled it; later, descendants of Neleus came there after displacement. Cleomenes first freed the Athenians from the sons of Pisistratus, then fought them as they defended their freedom and ravaged their territory. Athens suffered plague, was linked to traditions of Theseus, the Amazons, Pan, and Harpalus, and made Chalcinus and Dætus citizens after their return. It lost islands and naval supremacy after Philip’s treaties, endured Macedonian occupation, imposed rulers, and Lachares, then was liberated after Demetrius retained the Piraeus and fortified the Museum. Captured by Sulla after conflict with the Romans, it was injured by war but flourished again under Adrian. Its Odeum, Painted Chamber, Acropolis, theatre of Dionysus, temples, statues, tombs, public buildings, and monuments, including those of Olympian Zeus, Aphrodite, Æsculapius, Enyalius, and Wingless Victory, emphasize antiquity, religious practice, Persian victories, Theseus, and Athene.

Proserpine is a deity with a temple near Nine Springs, a temple at Sparta opposite Olympian Aphrodite’s, and statues with Demeter. She is honored with Demeter, Athene, and Poseidon in Lacius’s grove, and another statue stands in a former temple of Apollo. Sacred to the Rheti, she is described as Demeter’s daughter, carried away by Pluto; traditions connect the rape to Triptolemus, Demeter’s rites, Erineus, Lerna, and the Well of Flowers.

Triptolemus is represented by statues in temples near the Nine Springs and before the Eleusinium. Athenians and neighbouring tribes call him Celeus’s son and the first to sow corn; other traditions assign him to Ocean and Earth, Dysaules, or Rharus.

The Greeks suffered a general loss of freedom after the battle of Chaeronea, which made slaves of both those who were absent and those who fought against the Macedonians. Several Greek cities joined the Athenians against Macedonia, while the Bœotians in the former Theban territory supported the Macedonian interest.

l: rape of Proserpine, Description of Greece
s: The rape of Proserpine involves Demeter’s daughter being carried away by Pluto. It is associated with Demeter’s disguised arrival at the Well of Flowers and with Pluto’s descent to his underground realms at Erineus, marked by stones near the Chimarrus.
Eleusis is a city named for the hero Eleusis, with temples, the Well of Callichorus, and the Rharian plain; after battle it became associated with Athens while retaining its Mysteries.

Dysaules, said to be Celeus’s brother, came from Eleusis to Celeæ, perhaps not driven out by Ion, established Demeter’s mysteries there, and was buried there. Lines attributed to Orpheus name him father of Eubules and Triptolemus.

Laconia is a land and coastal region west of the Hermæ, formerly called Lelegia under Lelex. Its earliest rulers included Lelex, Myles, Eurotas, and Lacedæmon, followed later by Sparta’s kings. Lacedæmon first named the whole district, then the city originally called Sparta, whose government, market-place, temples, tombs, roads, and settlements are described. The region’s bays, towns, promontories, temples, and rivers are traced along its coast. Its border with Messenia was fixed at Gerenia by Augustus. Laconia supplies an invading army, suffers raids and plundering in conflict with Messenia, and is later connected with Lycurgus and war with Elis.

Marathon is a plain, said to be named from the hero Marathon, about equidistant from Athens and Carystus in Eubœa. Persians landed there and were defeated; the battle is depicted in the Painted Chamber. It honours Echetlæus and Hercules and preserves tombs and monuments for Athenians, Platæans, slaves, and Miltiades, along with a lake where fleeing Persians fell and a nearby cave of Pan.
Celestial Aphrodite, first worshipped by Assyrians, has Cythera's most holy and ancient Greek temple, where an old wooden armored statue stands; Phidias made a Parian stone statue.
Cythera lies opposite Bœæ near Platanistus, has Scandea harbour and a temple of Celestial Aphrodite.

drowned_at Acropolis [after seeing the ship with black sails] Ægeus was said to have drowned himself after seeing the ship returning from Crete with black sails, believing that Theseus had died. The Athenians maintained a hero-chapel in his memory, and the sea was visible from the shrine of Wingless Victory where he was said to have drowned.

Phidias, an Athenian son of Charmides and brother of Panænus, was a maker of statues. He made a brazen Athene from Marathon spoil, the Lemnian Athene, and the gold-and-ivory Zeus at Olympia, whose throne he decorated. His workshop worked on his statues, while others contributed shield carvings. An inscription identifies him as Zeus’s maker, and tradition says Zeus answered his prayer after the work was finished.
Miltiades, Athens’s archon and a Marathon general, failed to capture Paros, then died; his monument was at Marathon, where he was depicted in the Painted Chamber.

l: Temple of Theseus, Description of Greece
s: contains Theseus [as a temple painting subject] The Temple of Theseus contains paintings of the Athenians fighting the Amazons, Theseus fighting the Centaurs and Lapiths, and Theseus recovering Minos's ring from the sea. It is also connected with varying accounts of Theseus's adventures and death.
Pluto is linked to enclosed places at Hermione, including a place behind Chthonia’s temple and the Acherusian marsh; after the Rape of Proserpine, he is said to descend underground near Lerna.

Cimon son of Miltiades built part of the walls of the Acropolis. He also led picked Athenian men sent to aid the Lacedæmonians during the revolt of the Helots, though the Lacedæmonians sent them back because of suspicion.
Ilithyia, surnamed the Olympian, received many votive offerings at her temple on Mount Cronos and was jointly worshipped with Sosipolis for introducing him into the world.

Delos, formerly a Greek emporium thought to secure commerce because of Apollo, had a ship with nine banks of rowers. Menophanes attacked, killed inhabitants, robbed merchants and offerings, enslaved women and children, razed it, and cast Apollo’s statue into the sea.
Phædra becomes desperately, unsuccessfully enamoured of Hippolytus at Træzen, watches him train, and after rejection contrives his death; lovesickness alters a perforated myrtle.

Adrian builds Athens temples, especially Olympian Zeus's with a colossal ivory-and-gold statue, then temples to Hera, Pan-Hellenian Zeus, and all gods, and a gymnasium; he also restores horse-racing at Nemea's winter games for the Argives.

Thasos is the home of Theagenes and citizens who cast his statue into the sea. After famine, it sends envoys to Delphi, consults the Pythian Priestess again, recalls exiles, recovers and restores the statue, then sacrifices to it as a god.

l: temple of Olympian Zeus, Description of Greece
s: The Olympian Zeus temple, built by Adrian, contained a colossal ivory-and-gold Zeus and many statues and shrines. Its four-stade precinct, full of monuments, included flood traditions, an offering cavity, and statues of Adrian, colonial cities, Isocrates, and Persians.
Hebe is a goddess, identified at Phlius with Ganymeda, married to Hercules, whose ancient sanctuary with cypress grove grants complete immunity to suppliant slaves.
A river of Attica, sacred to the Muses and several gods, receives Eridanus, marks Orithyia’s abduction by the North Wind, and borders Herodes’s white-marble stadium.

l: theatre of Dionysus, Description of Greece
s: The theatre contained the most ancient temple of Dionysus, two shrines, statues, and paintings depicting myths involving Dionysus, Hephæstus, Pentheus, Lycurgus, Ariadne, and Theseus. Statues of tragic and comic dramatists, including Euripides, Sophocles, and Æschylus, were also displayed there.

Lycurgus is a legislator for the Lacedæmonians who, according to Herodotus, first served as regent for Labotas during his minority. Traditions traced his laws to Crete or connected them with Delphi. He legislated for the state and for youths’ fights, and changed human sacrifice at Artemis’s altar into the flogging of young men. After Alcander attacked him and he lost an eye, he was said to have built Athene the Eye-preserver’s temple. The Lacedæmonians honored him as a god with a temple, and his statue stood at Platanistas.

is_buried_at temple of Cretan Dionysus [according to the Argives] Ariadne was said to have been buried at the temple of Cretan Dionysus in Argos. Lyceas said that an earthenware cinerary urn containing her ashes was found there and seen by several Argives.

Sulla led the Roman capture of Athens during war against Mithridates, shut adversaries in the Ceramicus to be decimated by lot, was blamed for savagery, and burned the original imitation of Xerxes’ tent.

Mithridates, king of barbarians near the Euxine Sea, used Aristion as ambassador, fought Rome through Archelaus and Taxilus, won support from part of Athens, and was linked with Menophanes in Delos’s destruction. After Roman defeat and exile, he died by his own hand according to a divine interpretation, or was killed by a mercenary.
Aristion, Mithridates’ ambassador, persuaded Athenians to prefer Mithridates over Romans; after Roman victory, he fled to Athene’s temple, where Sulla seized and killed him.

Pythian Priestess, located at Delphi, gives answers and commands: she directs Corœbus, Elis, and Thasos, warns Glaucus about intended perjury, and identifies forgotten Theagenes as causing Thasos's divine wrath and dearth.
Sophocles, son of Leo, was a great light of Tragedy whose statue stood in the theatre; after his death, a dream reportedly honoured him and his plays as the new Siren.

Medusa is described either as Phorcus’s daughter, ruler near the Tritonian marsh, hunter, and battle leader, or as a wild Libyan woman who mistreated locals. Perseus treacherously killed her by night; her head was said to rest beneath a mound in Argos.

is_a woman [according to Procles’ rationalized account of Medusa] The Gorgon was identified with Medusa, whose monument and the tomb of Perseus were located near the market-place of Argos. The text says that the reason for her name was plain to the hearer, then recounts a tradition that she was the first woman to marry a second husband.

l: temple of Æsculapius, Description of Greece
s: contains Æsculapius [statues of the god and his sons are present] The temple of Æsculapius contained statues of the god and his sons, paintings, and a spring in which Halirrhothius was said to have drowned. It also displayed a Sarmatic coat of mail, prompting an account of Sarmatian armour made from horse hoofs.
